title: Default and named arguments
summary: A parameter can have a default value, used when the call leaves it out: def fine(days, rate=2). A call can name its values, fine(days=5, rate=3), so the order no longer matters and the call says what each number means. Values by position come first, named ones after; in a def, parameters with defaults come after the ones without.
objectives: Call a function with named (keyword) arguments.
Follow the order rules for calls and defs.
Choose defaults that make the common call short.

slides.h: By the end: one fine() for every case
slides.say: Meera runs the college library. Late books cost ₹2 a day, ₹5 for reference books, and never more than ₹100. By the end of this lesson one function will handle all three with a short call for the usual case.
points: A **default** is the value a parameter takes when the call leaves it out.
Write it in the def: `def fine(days, rate=2):`.
The call `fine(5)` uses rate 2; `fine(5, 5)` overrides it.

terms: the value a parameter has when the call doesn’t give one
a value given in a call; the parameter is its name inside the function

slides.say: Name a value in the call and Python matches it by name, not position. `fine(days=5, rate=5)` reads like a sentence, and the order no longer matters.
points: Use names when a call has several numbers that are easy to mix up.
Named arguments are also called **keyword arguments**.

slides.say: In a call, values by position come first and named ones after. In a def, parameters without defaults come first.
points: `fine(5, rate=3)` is fine; `fine(rate=3, 5)` is a SyntaxError.
`def due(title, days=14)` is fine; `def due(days=14, title)` is not.

slides.say: A `*` on its own in the def means “everything after this must be named”. Use it for options that would be confusing as bare values.
points: `report(books, True)` fails; `report(books, newest_first=True)` works and reads clearly.

slides.say: Make the default the case that happens most. Then most calls are short, and the unusual ones say what is different.
points: Don’t use a list or dict as a default: lesson 1.4 shows why.

demo.intro: Watch fine() grow a default rate and a cap.

steps.type:
def fine(days, rate):
    return days * rate

print(fine(5, 2))
print(fine(80, 2))

steps.say: Almost every call says 2. Make it the default, and cap the fine at ₹100.

steps.type:
def fine(days, rate=2, cap=100):
    return min(days * rate, cap)

demo.outro: Your turn: defaults for the usual case, names for the rest.

lab.intro: Defaults and named arguments. Sheetah calls your functions in ways you haven’t seen, so make every parameter work.

tasks.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Meera"))
print(greet("Ravi", "Namaste"))
tasks.explain: The second call overrides the default.

tasks.code:
def tag(title, shelf="A", copies=1):
    return f"{title}/{shelf}/{copies}"

print(tag("Godan", "C"))
print(tag("Godan", copies=3))
tasks.explain: "C" fills shelf by position; copies=3 by name.

tasks.prompt: Fill the gaps so **fine(4)** charges ₹2 a day and the second call charges ₹5 a day.

print(fine(4))
print(fine(4, __1__))
tasks.model:

print(fine(4))
print(fine(4, rate=5))
tasks.explain: A default in the def, a named value in the call.
hints: A default looks like name=value in the def.

print(due("The Guide", 7))

tasks.prompt: Write **fine(days, rate=2, cap=100)** that returns days × rate, but never more than cap. Sheetah calls it with values you haven’t seen.

quiz.q: Why name arguments in a call like `fine(days=5, rate=3)`?
options: The call says what each value means, and the order can’t be mixed up
a SyntaxError: positions must come before names
every parameter after it must be named in the call

points: `def fine(days, rate=2):` gives rate a default.
Positions first, names after; defaults after non-defaults.
A bare `*` makes the rest keyword-only.
